meta.title: Who really said "Make each day your masterpiece"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: John Wooden made it famous, but the line was printed in January 1931 — rule two of six for happiness, from a retired Supreme Court justice.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Make each day your masterpiece'?
meta.ogDescription: Not homespun Indiana wisdom. The line first appeared in a January 1931 magazine article distilling Justice John H. Clarke’s rules for happiness.

answer.label: Not John Wooden — a 1931 magazine article
answer.sourceLine: Historian Paul Putz traced the wording to “Help Yourself to Happiness,” a January 1931 piece in The American Magazine (Slate ↗) in which writer Merle Crowell condensed retired Supreme Court justice John H. Clarke’s advice into six rules — and “Make each day your masterpiece” is rule two. Wooden’s father Joshua copied the list; Wooden recited it for the rest of his life and, as late as 1956, still called it “An Adopted Creed.”

source.heading: The 1931 magazine page

docMeta.dd: Merle Crowell, from an interview with retired Supreme Court justice John H. Clarke
Copied by his father, Joshua Wooden; recited by the coach as “An Adopted Creed” in 1956

source.excerpt:
1. Be true to yourself.
2. Make each day your masterpiece.
3. Help others.
4. Drink deeply from good books.
5. Make friendship a fine art.
6. Build a shelter against a rainy day.
source.trailTitle: How six words became a family heirloom
trail: January 1931 — Writer Merle Crowell condenses retired justice John H. Clarke’s advice into six rules for happiness in The American Magazine. Rule two reads “Make each day your masterpiece.” Slate ↗
1956 — Wooden tells UCLA students about “An Adopted Creed,” which he says he has always carried in his wallet. He lists six points: no seventh, no mention of the Bible. Slate ↗

1966–1968 — In a devotional essay, a Guideposts reprint and a syndicated Lenten series, the creed gains a seventh point and a new origin: a card from his father on the day he finished eighth grade in Centerton, Indiana. Slate ↗
Late in life — Wooden is still reciting the line on television; Wikiquote files it among his sourced quotations with the note “quoting his father.” Wikiquote ↗
source.cutTag: Six rules, one of which travelled
source.excerptNote: Clarke’s six rules as reproduced from the January 1931 article by historian Paul Putz. Wooden’s familiar version reorders the list so that “Make each day your masterpiece” becomes point three, adds “especially the Bible” to the books line, and appends a seventh point about prayer and thanksgiving.

source.rightsHolder: Crowell Publishing Company, publisher of The American Magazine, and successors
source.rightsNote: “Help Yourself to Happiness” appeared in January 1931, so quotle.info treats it as in-copyright rather than assert a public-domain status it cannot prove. The picture is genuinely unsettled: Penn’s Online Books Page records no renewal for any issue of The American Magazine ↗ and dates its first renewed contribution to March 1931, not January — but no scan of that issue is freely available to check, and John Wooden’s own books and broadcasts, which are how almost everyone actually meets this line, remain firmly in copyright to his estate and publishers.

author.name: John H. Clarke
author.kicker: The man whose rules they were
author.heading: Whose six rules these are
author.bio: John Hessin Clarke sat on the United States Supreme Court from October 1916 until September 1922, when he stepped down — in Slate’s summary of the episode, to live a less strenuous life of travel and contemplation. In January 1931 The American Magazine ran a profile that boiled his hard-won advice down to six numbered rules for happiness. One of those six outlived every opinion he wrote: it was copied onto a card in Indiana and became, a generation later, the most quoted line in American coaching.

cite.sourceCitation: Merle Crowell, “Help Yourself to Happiness,” The American Magazine, January 1931 — identified as the source of the Wooden family creed in Paul Putz, “John Wooden’s Homespun Creed Was Not So Homespun,” Slate, 17 May 2017.

copyAttribution: “Make each day your masterpiece.” — not originally John Wooden. The line was printed as rule two of six in Merle Crowell's article “Help Yourself to Happiness,” The American Magazine, January 1931, distilled from an interview with retired Supreme Court Justice John H. Clarke. Wooden's father Joshua copied the list; Wooden recited it for decades and called it “An Adopted Creed” in 1956. Via Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and who earned it
misattribution.intro: Nearly every poster, mug and locker-room placard credits this to John Wooden. A more careful tier of sources credits his father, Joshua. Both are downstream of the same magazine page.

items.why: Wooden recited the creed from at least 1956 until his death in 2010 and printed it in his books, but he never claimed authorship — he always credited his father. The words reached him third-hand. Slate ↗

The coaching literature treats the seven-point creed as the original philosophy of a self-educated Indiana farmer. Putz found that Joshua copied it from the 1931 article — and his son’s own 1956 phrasing, “An Adopted Creed … which I have always carried in my wallet,” concedes as much. Slate ↗

items.who: A card handed over at an eighth-grade graduation in Centerton, Indiana
items.why: That account appears in Wooden’s writing only from 1966 onward. The creed was not published until January 1931, by which point Wooden — born in 1910 — was an undergraduate at Purdue. Slate ↗, Wikipedia ↗

Wooden’s 1956 recitation had six points and no religious language. The seventh point about prayer and thanksgiving, and the words “especially the Bible” on point four, are additions that appear in the devotional retellings of the 1960s. Slate ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The wording belongs to a January 1931 American Magazine article by Merle Crowell, presenting six rules for happiness drawn from an interview with retired Supreme Court justice John H. Clarke. Slate ↗

context.heading: Why the line outran its source
lead: The six words survive because of what John Wooden did with them, not where they came from. He kept the creed on a folded card in his wallet, taught it to players and later to executives, and by the time he died in 2010 it had become the most portable piece of his philosophy — short enough for a gym wall, warm enough for a commencement address.

What Putz’s find changes is the frame, not the advice. Read in its original setting — a self-improvement feature written for The American Magazine’s middle-class readership of more than two million — “Make each day your masterpiece” is a piece of Depression-era success literature aimed at businessmen, not folk wisdom handed down on an Indiana farm.
context.detailsSummary: Why the origin story changed in the 1960s
detailsBody: Putz argues the retelling did cultural work. Between 1964 and 1968 Wooden’s UCLA teams began their championship run just as campus protest peaked, and — in a phrase from biographer Johnny Smith quoted in the Slate account ↗ — the coach came to project an “image of consensus in a period of dissent.” A creed handed over at a country grade school in Centerton, Indiana suited that role rather better than one clipped from a national magazine.

There is a smaller irony in the record. When Pat Williams asked Wooden’s former players what they remembered about the seven-point creed, most of them did not recall hearing about it during their playing days; the creed found its real audience in the business books that followed his 1972 autobiography — which is roughly the readership The American Magazine had written it for in the first place.
context.pull: Wooden called it “An Adopted Creed” in 1956. By 1968 it had become his father’s.

sourcesVerified.claim: "Make each day your masterpiece" is rule two of six in Merle Crowell's article "Help Yourself to Happiness," The American Magazine, January 1931, based on an interview with former Supreme Court justice John H. Clarke; Joshua Wooden copied the creed from it; a 1956 Los Angeles Times article quotes Wooden calling it "An Adopted Creed" carried in his wallet with only six points and no Bible reference; the eighth-grade-graduation origin story appears in Wooden's writing from 1966 onward; Wooden was born in 1910 and was enrolled at Purdue in 1931.
Wikiquote's John Wooden page lists "Make each day your masterpiece." in its sourced quotations, under an interview on Charlie Rose, annotated "quoting his father."
John Hessin Clarke was born 18 September 1857, died 22 March 1945, and served as an Associate Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court from 9 October 1916 to 18 September 1922, resigning in 1922.
John Wooden was born 14 October 1910 in Hall, Indiana, died 4 June 2010, and attended Purdue from 1929 to 1932.

The Online Books Page copyright record for The American Magazine states "First renewed issue: no issue renewals found in CCE or CPRS" and "First renewed contribution in: March 1931 (v. 111 no. 3)", with the renewal list covering all active contribution renewals through 1935.

thewoodeneffect.com, bylined to Craig Impelman and describing him as "Coach Wooden's grandson-in-law" (footer: "John R. Wooden™ owned and licensed by John Wooden Legacy LLC"), presents "Make each day your masterpiece" as the third item in the list of "Seven Things to Do" given to Coach Wooden by his father, later known as the Seven Point Creed.
The American Magazine was published by Crowell Publishing Company, Merle Crowell was its editor from 1923 to 1929 (succeeded by Sumner Blossom), and its last issue was August 1956.
The Online Books Page serial record shows free HathiTrust coverage of The American Magazine running to volume 110 (1930), so the January 1931 issue is not freely available online.
